doc.title: Glenn Zottola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 7, 2020

title: Perfect pitch, transposing instruments and avoiding theory
summary: How perfect pitch works across alto, tenor and trumpet, and why he never learned theory.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me ask you a question before I forget it. You said you had perfect pitch as a kid.
I don’t have it. And I’m wondering —
You don’t have to. I mean a lot of guys that are amazing don’t have it you know.

Yeah. But I’m wondering how does it work when you’re playing, I mean you play the alto sax and tenor and trumpet so with a concert pitch you’ve got potentially three things going. If you’re playing an E flat horn you’re not, the notes you’re playing on the sax are not concert pitch. So does this cause some kind of scrambling in your brain?

It’s a good question. Realize something, okay? I know nothing about chords and I have no awareness of what key I’m playing in. Okay? So it’s all here. I’m hearing the music. Now if, sometimes I remember in the beginning when I had switched to alto and then to go tenor or trumpet, going to the E flat there might be, because I’m pressing down a C, right, on the alto. And for perfect pitch it’s not the C I’m used to on a B flat instrument. Right? So there was a little adjustment there, but then I just started thinking about it and used my ears. Relative, you know.
Yeah. Did you ever feel compelled — I’m trying to phrase this question — in different musical situations that man I ought to learn some theory?

You know I wanted to when I was a kid. I went to — I almost failed it, I went to a theory course in high school and I was going crazy. I went to my dad and I said, ‘cause they were teaching stationary Do. No they were teaching Movable Do.

Yeah. My dad started me off on solfeggio [claps] you know. So to me a C is a C carved in stone. And they were trying to teach me chords where the root was this and it’s not a C anymore, and with the perfect pitch I was going crazy with that. So I went to a friend of mine, a really good jazz pianist and I said you know, “I really want to learn theory and I’m having a lot of trouble.” And he said, “Let me just tell you something, you’re already playing all these changes, don’t do it, it’s going to ruin your playing.” That was his advice. I mean not great advice but that’s what he — “you’re already playing all this stuff.” I said, “Yeah but I’d like to know what a minor seventh is, whatever that is.” He said, “You’re already playing minor sevenths.” You know.
Yes. “I feel as though I have to call it something.”
Yeah, right, right, right. I was talking to Chick Corea about that because you know he’s very knowledgeable, you know.
Yeah. Well I have a Chick Corea question for later but we haven’t got there yet.
So all these opportunities were coming your way and this is sort of a follow-up to the question about choosing a career.
